derived: Vertex generated $12,074mm of free cash flow on $49,396mm of revenue over the five years to 2025, a 24.44% margin, against the 33.0% its cost of sales, SG&A and R&D leave. Five years rather than three because operating cash flow was negative $493mm in 2024 on the Alpine acquisition, which takes a three-year window to 17.5% and lets one deal set the rate. Solved so the modelled book reproduces the margin rather than taken off a single line. Restated before interest: VRTX paid $195mm of interest inside operating cash flow over 2021 to 2025, 0.39% of revenue. The free cash flow above is struck after it and the valuation already charges the debt by subtracting net debt, so the charge falls by that much, from 10.33% to 9.94%. Restated at replacement capex: VRTX spent $1,375mm on plant over 2021 to 2025 against $758mm of plant depreciation, 1.25% of revenue above what keeps the plant running. Taken at depreciation, the charge falls from 9.94% to 8.47%. Restated without one-off cash: VRTX's free cash flow over 2021 to 2025 carried $6,517mm of deal payments in operating cash flow, capital allocation whose assets the book values separately. None recurs, so the charge falls from 8.47% to 0.00%. Restated to the amortisation floor: the filed cost lines leave a 39.05% pre-tax margin where the cash over 2021 to 2025 supports 43.77%, so the charge rebuilds at -4.72%. It was held at nil, but VRTX books $20mm of non-cash amortisation of acquired intangibles inside cost of sales in FY2025 (0000875320-26-000056), 0.17% of revenue, so the charge stops at that floor: -0.17%. Restated without working capital build: over 2021 to 2025 VRTX's cash flow statement shows receivables up $1,164mm, inventories up $1,594mm, payables up $288mm, a working capital build of $2,470mm, 5.00% of revenue. Growth ties that cash up once, not on every product for ever, so the charge was held at the amortisation floor, -0.17% where the filed figures rebuild it at -4.72%, and stays there.

column11: pregabalin, the last new mechanism to reach DPNP with a measured share: of 12,074 US adults first diagnosed with DPN over 2006 to 2011 who started a DPNP medicine, 21.6% started pregabalin (Yang M, Qian C, Liu Y, Pain Med 2015;16(11):2075-2083, PMID 26118704, MarketScan), the anchor lly_ly4065967.csv and the Journavx DPN row use. MULTIPLE 0.25, A JUDGEMENT: 0.25 x 21.6% = 5.4% of the pool on the drug, half the 0.5 the Journavx DPN row gives suzetrigine. The pool is each year's cohort, so the steady stock is peak x pool / 0.745, and a stock of 5.4% needs a peak of 0.054 x 0.745 = 0.04023. Why a quarter: Vertex says VX-993 was 'powered to determine whether VX-993 would result in higher clinical efficacy than previously demonstrated with the NaV1.8 pathway', and on missing that bar in acute pain 'we did not expect VX-993 to be superior to suzetrigine and therefore chose not to further advance VX-993 as monotherapy in acute pain' (10-K 0000875320-26-000056). So VX-993 reaches DPN only as a better suzetrigine, launching about four years after it
column12: TWO VERTEX LAYERS ON ONE POOL, AND HOW THEY ARE KEPT APART: this row and the Journavx Diabetic Neuropathies layer draw on the same 1,822,186 patients, in two files, and the engine sums them without knowing they overlap. If VX-993 succeeds it will largely take suzetrigine's patients, Vertex's own substitution rather than new share, so the two are not additive: the quarter multiple is the part of the class a better NaV1.8 could add, and reading this asset's value on top of the full Journavx DPN layer counts some patients twice. Settled by sales, not by an event
